questions.question: Compare resource preemption and resource ordering as methods of deadlock prevention.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare resource preemption and resource ordering as methods of deadlock
  • prevention.
  • Answer: ((1 mark) for each point)

  • • Releasing/preempting held resources when an additional request cannot be
  • satisfied, with reacquisition before the process continues ((1 mark)).

  • memory); limitations for other resources (printers, tape drives) ((1 mark)).

  • and requiring acquisition in increasing order ((1 mark)).

  • sequence of resource requests ((1 mark)).

questions.question: a) Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose. b) Explain the steps followed by the Banker’s Safety Algorithm to determine whether the system is safe.
questions.solution_html:
• a) Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose.
  • b) Explain the steps followed by the Banker’s Safety Algorithm to determine whether
  • the system is safe.
  • Answer: (a) (7 marks); (b) (8 marks)
  • (a) Data structures and their purposes ((7 marks))
  • • Define n processes and m resource types; identify appropriate vector/matrix
  • dimensions ((1 mark)).
  • • Available: m-element vector giving currently available instances of each resource
  • type ((1 mark)).
  • • Max: n × m matrix giving each process’s declared maximum demand ((1 mark)).
  • • Allocation: n × m matrix giving resources currently assigned to each process (1
  • mark).
  • • Need: n × m matrix giving each process’s remaining possible demand ((1 mark)).
  • • Relationship: Need[i, j] = Max[i, j] - Allocation[i, j] ((1 mark)).
  • • Temporary Work and Finish structures used by the safety test ((1 mark)).
  • (b) Safety Algorithm ((8 marks))
  • • Initialise Work = Available ((1 mark)).
  • • Initialise Finish[i] = false for every process ((1 mark)).
  • • Find an unfinished process i such that Needᵢ ≤ Work for every resource type (2
  • marks).
  • • Simulate completion: Work = Work + Allocationᵢ and set Finish[i] = true ((2 marks)).
  • • Repeat until all processes finish or no eligible unfinished process remains ((1 mark)).
  • • If all Finish values are true, the state is safe; otherwise it is unsafe. An unsafe state
  • is not necessarily already deadlocked ((1 mark)).
  • Note: Accept correct pseudocode or a clearly explained sequence of steps. No numerical example is
  • compulsory.
questions.final_answer: Option Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose.

questions.question: A logical address in a segmentation system is given as 2400. The segment table contains the following entries: Segment Base Limit 0 1000 500 1 4000 800 2 6000 1000 3 8000 600 Use the segment table to determine whether the given logical address is valid and, if valid, calculate its corresponding physical address. Explain the steps involved in the address translation.
questions.solution_html:
• A logical address in a segmentation system is given as 2400. The segment table contains
  • the following entries: Segment 0 (Base 1000, Limit 500), Segment 1 (Base 4000, Limit
  • 800), Segment 2 (Base 6000, Limit 1000), Segment 3 (Base 8000, Limit 600). Use the
  • segment table to determine whether the given logical address is valid and, if valid
  • calculate its corresponding physical address. Explain the steps involved in the address
  • translation.
  • Answer: ((3 marks) for each point)
  • • A segmented logical address consists of a pair (s, d), where s is the segment
  • number and d is the offset ((3 marks)).
  • • Identifies that the encoding convention is not given and explains the ambiguity of
  • the address 2400 ((3 marks)).
  • • Segment-table lookup: s indexes the table; Base gives the starting physical address
  • and Limit gives the segment length ((3 marks)).
  • • Validity checks: 0 ≤ s < 4 and 0 ≤ d < Limit; an invalid segment number or an
  • offset beyond the limit causes an addressing/protection trap ((3 marks)).
  • • Translation rule: Physical address = Base + d, with the conclusion: no unique
  • numerical result as printed; alternatively, 6400 under an explicitly stated segment
  • 2/offset-400 assumption ((3 marks)).
  • Conditional numerical answer: If the candidate explicitly assumes that 2400 represents
  • segment 2, offset 400
  • • Segment 2 has Base 6000 and Limit 1000.
  • • Offset 400 < 1000, hence the address is valid.
  • • Physical address = 6000 + 400 = 6400.
  • Note: The logical address is printed as 2400 without a segment number–offset pair or an encoding
  • convention, so it does not determine a unique answer. A complete answer explaining the ambiguity
  • validity checks and translation method may receive full marks without inventing a numerical
  • interpretation. Do not treat 6400 as the sole compulsory answer. Final treatment of this question
  • should follow the examination authority’s approved instruction.
  • General Instructions to Examiners
  • • Follow the question paper’s distribution: 10 + 30 + 30 = (70 marks).
  • • Award credit for technically correct equivalent wording.
  • • Award proportionate partial marks for correct concepts and intermediate steps.
  • • Do not insist on programs, diagrams or examples unless needed to demonstrate the
  • requested concept.
questions.final_answer: Option (d) , where s is the segment

questions.question: a) Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose. b) Explain the steps followed by the Banker’s Safety Algorithm to determine whether the system is safe.
questions.solution_html:
• a) Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose.
  • b) Explain the steps followed by the Banker’s Safety Algorithm to determine whether
  • the system is safe.
  • Answer: (a) (7 marks); (b) (8 marks)
  • (a) Data structures and their purposes ((7 marks))
  • • Define n processes and m resource types; identify appropriate vector/matrix
  • dimensions ((1 mark)).
  • • Available: m-element vector giving currently available instances of each resource
  • type ((1 mark)).
  • • Max: n × m matrix giving each process’s declared maximum demand ((1 mark)).
  • • Allocation: n × m matrix giving resources currently assigned to each process (1
  • mark).
  • • Need: n × m matrix giving each process’s remaining possible demand ((1 mark)).
  • • Relationship: Need[i, j] = Max[i, j] - Allocation[i, j] ((1 mark)).
  • • Temporary Work and Finish structures used by the safety test ((1 mark)).
  • (b) Safety Algorithm ((8 marks))
  • • Initialise Work = Available ((1 mark)).
  • • Initialise Finish[i] = false for every process ((1 mark)).
  • • Find an unfinished process i such that Needᵢ ≤ Work for every resource type (2
  • marks).
  • • Simulate completion: Work = Work + Allocationᵢ and set Finish[i] = true ((2 marks)).
  • • Repeat until all processes finish or no eligible unfinished process remains ((1 mark)).
  • • If all Finish values are true, the state is safe; otherwise it is unsafe. An unsafe state
  • is not necessarily already deadlocked ((1 mark)).
  • Note: Accept correct pseudocode or a clearly explained sequence of steps. No numerical example is
  • compulsory.
questions.final_answer: Option Describe the data structures used by Banker’s Algorithm and explain their purpose.

questions.question: A logical address in a segmentation system is given as 2400. The segment table contains the following entries: Segment Base Limit 0 1000 500 1 4000 800 2 6000 1000 3 8000 600 Use the segment table to determine whether the given logical address is valid and, if valid, calculate its corresponding physical address. Explain the steps involved in the address translation.
questions.solution_html:
• A logical address in a segmentation system is given as 2400. The segment table contains
  • the following entries: Segment 0 (Base 1000, Limit 500), Segment 1 (Base 4000, Limit
  • 800), Segment 2 (Base 6000, Limit 1000), Segment 3 (Base 8000, Limit 600). Use the
  • segment table to determine whether the given logical address is valid and, if valid
  • calculate its corresponding physical address. Explain the steps involved in the address
  • translation.
  • Answer: ((3 marks) for each point)
  • • A segmented logical address consists of a pair (s, d), where s is the segment
  • number and d is the offset ((3 marks)).
  • • Identifies that the encoding convention is not given and explains the ambiguity of
  • the address 2400 ((3 marks)).
  • • Segment-table lookup: s indexes the table; Base gives the starting physical address
  • and Limit gives the segment length ((3 marks)).
  • • Validity checks: 0 ≤ s < 4 and 0 ≤ d < Limit; an invalid segment number or an
  • offset beyond the limit causes an addressing/protection trap ((3 marks)).
  • • Translation rule: Physical address = Base + d, with the conclusion: no unique
  • numerical result as printed; alternatively, 6400 under an explicitly stated segment
  • 2/offset-400 assumption ((3 marks)).
  • Conditional numerical answer: If the candidate explicitly assumes that 2400 represents
  • segment 2, offset 400
  • • Segment 2 has Base 6000 and Limit 1000.
  • • Offset 400 < 1000, hence the address is valid.
  • • Physical address = 6000 + 400 = 6400.
  • Note: The logical address is printed as 2400 without a segment number–offset pair or an encoding
  • convention, so it does not determine a unique answer. A complete answer explaining the ambiguity
  • validity checks and translation method may receive full marks without inventing a numerical
  • interpretation. Do not treat 6400 as the sole compulsory answer. Final treatment of this question
  • should follow the examination authority’s approved instruction.
  • General Instructions to Examiners
  • • Follow the question paper’s distribution: 10 + 30 + 30 = (70 marks).
  • • Award credit for technically correct equivalent wording.
  • • Award proportionate partial marks for correct concepts and intermediate steps.
  • • Do not insist on programs, diagrams or examples unless needed to demonstrate the
  • requested concept.
questions.final_answer: Option (d) , where s is the segment
